newsitem.title: UK: BOE to help develop TARGET even if denied credit.
newsitem.headline: BOE to help develop TARGET even if denied credit.

text.p: The Bank of England will continue to participate in development of the planned single European currency payments system, even if the UK is denied access to intraday credit, deputy director John Townend said. Some countries, such as Germany, are unhappy about allowing those outside the launch of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) full access to intraday euro liquidity, fearing this will disrupt attempts to control European monetary policy. "There's no question of our saying we're going to pull out of the project..we will continue to work towards an effective conclusion to TARGET," Townend told Reuters.
The UK is making a major technical contribution to the development of TARGET (Trans-European Automated Real-time Gross Settlement Express Transfer), Townend said.
"It's a strategic objective for the UK to continue to participate in the discussions. We continue to have the aim of linking to TARGET -- that's absolutely what we intend," he said.
The BOE has repeatedly said it sees no monetary policy issues arising from the provision of intraday credit, so long as this does not spill over significantly into overnight liquidity.
There was no sign yet of a resolution to the liquidity issue, Townend said.

"There must be a possibility that despite our desire to have this issue resolved pretty quickly...it may not be resolved and it might be left to the ECB (European Central Bank) itself to decide when it is formed in 1998."
This means that only countries which take part in the launch of EMU will have a say in the issue.
If Britain were to remain outside the first wave of EMU and were denied full access to liquidity, the BOE would consider developing an alternative payments system, said Townend.

"On the outside, you could still develop a euro payments system which would be effective, would link to TARGET but which would not need intraday access to central accounts. You could generate your own liquidity on the outside," he said.
Townend gave no further details. Earlier, he said if non-EMU banks were denied full access to TARGET, use of the system would be more costly.
